core: Orchestra as a coordinated instrumental ensemble in an introductory Western symphony-orchestra context
Strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion as common family sections
How differing family timbres and ranges can support listening for lines, layers, and contrast
supporting: Variation in orchestral forces by repertoire, historical period, and individual work
The difference between an instrument family, an ensemble section, and a specific musical role
A listening method that describes audible evidence before identifying a precise instrument
outOfScope: Detailed seating charts, score order, audition guidance, or conducting technique
A historical survey of every orchestra or a full history of the symphony
Claims that particular families have fixed emotions, rankings, or permanent musical jobs
Treating the Western symphony-orchestra model as a universal ensemble structure

claims.claim: For the introductory Western symphony-orchestra context used here, an orchestra coordinates instrumental performers from common families including strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.
The New South Wales Department of Education resource treats strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion as the four families of the Western symphony orchestra.

The cited LOUIS discussion of the Classical Period says strings remained a sound foundation while additional woodwinds, brass, and percussion appeared, and it notes that orchestral forces were expanded to bring out contrasting tone colors.
An instrument family is not the same as a single musical role: instruments and sections can support melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, or contrast depending on the arrangement.
A listener can describe orchestral sound responsibly by identifying a broad family and audible feature before claiming a precise instrument or expressive meaning.
The four-family symphony-orchestra grouping is a contextual learning tool, not a complete or universal structure for ensembles across all musical traditions.
